messages.content:
You are proposing scientific conjectures. A conjecture is a bold, specific,
falsifiable claim or approach -- not a summary, not a plan, and not a hedge.
Write plainly.

Why do long-running software systems become harder to change over time, even when every individual change was reviewed, tested, and locally correct?

Stay within this direction: Information-theoretic growth of required context to certify change-safety

Generate 10 candidate conjectures within that direction, sampled from the
full distribution of responses you could give. For each, give the
conjecture and your estimated probability that it is the response you would
give to this prompt. Every candidate's probability must be below 0.10.
Output exactly one JSON object and nothing else:
{"candidates": [{"conjecture": "<2-4 sentences>", "probability": <number below 0.10>}, ... 10 items]}

message.content: {"candidates": [{"conjecture": "The mutual information between a code element and the set of all downstream consumers grows superlinearly with system age, so certifying a change requires verifying a information-space whose dimensionality exceeds any individual reviewer's working memory capacity.", "probability": 0.07}, {"conjecture": "Each locally correct change increases the Kolmogorov complexity of the minimal proof that the system is safe, because the proof must reference all prior changes; eventually the proof length exceeds the system's own description length, making safety certification uncomputable in practice.", "probability": 0.06}, {"conjecture": "The entropy of the implicit invariant set—assumptions that hold but are never asserted—grows monotonically with each change, so the information needed to rule out invariant violations in a new change diverges from what is recoverable from code and tests alone.", "probability": 0.08}, {"conjecture": "Change-safety certification is fundamentally a channel capacity problem: the rate at which a developer can absorb relevant context is bounded, while the rate at which new context is generated by prior changes grows linearly, so eventually every change exceeds the developer's information absorption rate.", "probability": 0.05}, {"conjecture": "The number of distinct execution paths that can reach a given code element grows exponentially with the number of prior changes due to combinatorial interaction effects, so the information required to certify that a change is safe across all paths grows exponentially even when each change is locally simple.", "probability": 0.04}, {"conjecture": "Each locally correct change adds information to the system but rarely removes any, so the Shannon entropy of the system's behavioral specification grows monotonically; certifying a change requires distinguishing the new behavior from all prior behaviors, an O(n) information-theoretic lookup that grows with system history.", "probability": 0.09}, {"conjecture": "The minimal test suite needed to certify change-safety has information content that grows as the log of the number of distinct state configurations reachable by the system, and this state space grows multiplicatively with each change that introduces new state variables or interactions.", "probability": 0.03}, {"conjecture": "The description length of the weakest precondition required to prove a change is safe grows monotonically because each prior change can add new disjuncts to that precondition; eventually the precondition is too long for any reviewer to hold in working memory and verify against the code.", "probability": 0.06}, {"conjecture": "Each change that is locally correct but not globally certified creates an information debt—an implicit constraint that future changes must respect—so the number of unstated constraints grows linearly with changes, and the information cost of checking all constraints for a new change grows quadratically.", "probability": 0.07}, {"conjecture": "The information-theoretic distance between the system's actual behavior and its documented specification grows with each locally correct change, because each change optimizes locally without updating global documentation; certifying safety requires bridging this gap, and the cost grows with the gap's entropy.", "probability": 0.05}]}
